common_name: Tikumu Mountain Daisy (Large Silver-Leaved NZ Alpine Daisy)

planting.note: Set divisions or young plants into a gritty, humus-rich scree or rockery in spring so roots establish before the first hot stretch of summer.

directions: This South Island tussock-grassland daisy forms a bold rosette of leathery, silver-backed sword leaves topped by white, yellow-centered daisy flowers on stout stalks in early summer. It needs a cool, open position with sharp drainage and steady moisture at the root, since it comes from high-rainfall mountain herbfields rather than dry rock gardens. Gardeners in hot-summer regions should treat it as a specialist scree or trough subject, since prolonged heat and humidity quickly rot the crown even when drainage is good. Established clumps slowly spread by rhizome and can be divided to increase stock.
sources: Alpine Garden Society Encyclopaedia of Alpines

planting.note: Plant in spring in gritty, free-draining soil with some summer moisture; avoid planting into heavy, waterlogged ground.

directions: Cotton daisy carries narrow, leathery leaves backed with dense white felt, forming wide mats that send up white, yellow-centered daisy flowers on woolly stalks in early summer. It thrives in cool maritime climates with mild winters and summers that rarely turn hot, conditions that mimic its tussock-grassland home in the South Island high country. Large clumps can degenerate in the center over time, especially where air circulation is poor, so periodic division keeps plantings vigorous. Cutting back spent flower stems promptly often encourages a smaller second flush later in the season.

planting.note: Cold-stratify fresh seed for 4-6 weeks before sowing so germination coincides with the cool conditions this species demands.

directions: Despite its common name this is not a lily but the largest buttercup in the world, carrying glossy rounded leaves and masses of large white, yellow-stamened flowers above South Island subalpine herbfields. It demands constant moisture in a gravelly, fast-draining mix and consistently cool temperatures, making it a genuine challenge outside mild, high-rainfall climates with cool summers. Full sun suits it where summers stay cool, but a little afternoon shade helps where heat builds up. Because it resents root disturbance, it is best raised from fresh seed and transplanted while still young rather than divided.

common_name: Hunangamoho Snow Tussock (Plumed NZ Tussock Grass)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in free-draining, humus-rich soil and expect slow establishment during the first season.

directions: Hunangamoho forms a dense mound of broad, deep-green arching leaves tinged coppery with age, sending up tall, showy plumes of cream to golden seed heads in summer that persist well into winter. It tolerates drought once its roots are established but performs best with regular moisture and free drainage during its first year or two. Groom old foliage by combing through the clump with gloved hands in late winter rather than shearing it back hard, which can damage the growing point. It works well as a specimen grass or massed planting in coastal and native-themed gardens.

subcategory: New Zealand alpine architectural rosette perennial

planting.note: Set young plants directly into their permanent spot, since large speargrasses resent transplanting once the deep taproot is established; mulch with stone chips to keep the crown cool.

directions: The giant speargrass is the largest of New Zealand's fearsome Aciphylla tribe, building a clump of rigid, razor-tipped compound leaves to about half a metre tall, with male and female flowers on separate plants rising on flower spikes that can reach several metres in a wet mountain season. It wants a sunny, permanent position with sharp drainage and a deep, gritty root run, since the woody taproot resents disturbance once established. Give it space and keep it away from paths and play areas, since the leaf tips are genuinely sharp enough to puncture skin and clothing. Its dramatic silhouette makes it a strong accent plant or living barrier in a large native or gravel garden.
sources: Te Ara - The Encyclopedia of New Zealand

planting.note: Plant into a raised, gritty, lime-free scree or trough in spring, angling the site so winter rain drains away quickly from the crown.

directions: Vegetable sheep forms a tight, rock-hard looking mat of minute silver-grey leaves packed so densely that from a distance it resembles a sleeping animal draped over the ground or a boulder. It is cold-hardy but far more easily killed by winter wet than by frost, so cultivation outside its native fell-fields almost always means a raised trough, scree bed, or pot kept under cover from autumn rain. Give it poor, gritty, non-calcareous soil and full sun, and resist the urge to feed or water it generously once established, since lush conditions cause the tight cushion to rot or open up. It is slow but very drought-tolerant once its mat has knit together.
sources: Alpine Garden Society Encyclopaedia of Alpines

common_name: Creeping Mountain Foxglove (Dwarf NZ Alpine Ourisia)
subcategory: New Zealand alpine creeping mat perennial

planting.note: Plant into a cool, lightly shaded scree or trough with constantly moist, gritty soil; avoid hot, dry spots where the fine creeping stems scorch.

directions: This diminutive relative of the foxglove creeps along the ground on fine, mostly hairless stems set with small notched leaves, producing short stalks of white, yellow-eyed flowers from late spring into autumn in its native alpine herbfields. It prefers a cool, lightly shaded site with soil that never dries out, making it a good candidate for a shaded trough or the cooler side of an alpine scree bed rather than an open, baking rockery. Because it spreads by creeping rather than forming a single crown, established mats can be gently teased apart and replanted to increase stock. It is a true specialist alpine best suited to growers who can offer consistent cool moisture through summer.

planting.note: Cold-stratify seed for about four weeks, then sow in a deep, moist, peaty and gritty mix; only ever propagate from seed or cuttings, never by removing plants from the wild.

directions: Mountain gentian is a branching New Zealand alpine herb with narrow, deep green to reddish leaves and clean white flowers held just above the foliage from mid-summer into autumn, found naturally in subalpine to high-alpine ground across the North and South Islands. It is a genuine specialist plant, needing deep, constantly moist, peaty and gritty soil to mimic the seepage zones of its native herbfields, and most growers find it a demanding subject outside a dedicated alpine bed. Seed germinates readily without pretreatment but responds well to a short cold period followed by warmth. Because wild populations should never be disturbed, all garden stock should trace back to nursery-grown seed or cuttings.
sources: Royal New Zealand Institute of Horticulture

planting.note: Wedge young plants into a vertical limestone crevice, tufa block, or wall in spring, since this species needs sharp drainage around its rosette to avoid rot.

directions: Pyrenean saxifrage spends its first several years building a single, perfect rosette of narrow, lime-encrusted silver leaves that can reach a foot across, then sends up one spectacular fountain-shaped spike crowded with hundreds of small white flowers before the rosette dies. Because each plant flowers only once, it is best grown as a crevice or tufa specimen where seedlings can be allowed to self-sow and replace their parents over time. It needs alkaline to neutral, sharply drained soil that nonetheless never dries out completely, and full sun suits it in cool climates while a little shade from the hottest afternoon sun helps where summers run warm. Gardeners in hot regions should expect to raise replacements regularly rather than treat any single rosette as permanent.

planting.note: Root single rosette cuttings in early summer and plant into a vertical crevice, tufa wall, or scree trough with acidic, gritty soil the following spring.

directions: This tiny cushion-former grows naturally on granite cliffs above 2,500 meters in the Pyrenees, favoring acidic rock rather than the limestone most of its relatives prefer, and bears small white, yellow-eyed flowers held just above its hairy grey-green rosettes in spring. It is one of the easier true high alpines to flower well, typically performing strongly for three or four years before patches of the cushion begin to die back, which is normal rather than a sign of poor culture. Growing it in a scree bed, alpine trough, or sheltered crevice with gritty, well-drained, acidic soil gives the best results, and renewing stock periodically from rooted rosette cuttings keeps a planting looking full. Full sun and excellent drainage are essential; standing winter wet is its biggest enemy.
sources: Alpine Garden Society Encyclopaedia of Alpines

planting.note: Sow or transplant in spring into free-draining, alkaline soil in a sunny rockery; avoid rich or waterlogged ground, which shortens its life.

directions: Pyrenean pink forms a low, wiry mat of narrow blue-green foliage studded in spring and summer with small, sweetly scented pink flowers, native to rocky slopes and meadows of the western Pyrenees. It wants the same conditions as most rock garden dianthus: full sun, free-draining, slightly alkaline soil, and average but not excessive moisture, since wet feet in winter are its main vulnerability. Trimming spent flowering stems back after bloom helps keep the mat compact and encourages repeat flowering later in the season. It suits a sunny crevice, trough, or wall top where its scent can be appreciated at close range.

planting.note: Surface-sow seed in fall for natural winter stratification, or refrigerate seed for 6-8 weeks before an early spring sowing; the fine seed needs light to germinate so do not cover it.

directions: Alpine poppy makes a tidy, dwarf clump of finely cut blue-green foliage topped by papery, satin-textured flowers in white, yellow, or orange, opening over a long season from spring onward. It needs deep, fast-draining but not dry soil and a genuine cold winter dormancy to perform well, which is why it struggles and often fails outright south of about USDA zone 6. In hot-summer regions a little light afternoon shade helps extend the display, but good drainage matters more than shade for keeping the crown alive. Because individual plants are short-lived, letting a few seed heads mature and self-sow each year keeps a planting going indefinitely.

planting.note: Plant into a sheltered, humus-rich, well-drained but moisture-retentive bed in spring; this species resents both drought and waterlogging.

directions: Spotted gentian is an upright alpine meadow gentian of the Carpathians and other Central and Southeastern European ranges, bearing pale yellow, bell-shaped flowers marked with small purplish-brown spots clustered along the upper stem in summer. It grows naturally at elevations above about 1,500 meters and wants a cool, humid site with consistently moist yet well-drained, slightly acidic soil rather than a hot, dry rockery. It is not a common nursery item and is best sourced as seed through alpine plant society seed exchanges, then grown on for a couple of seasons before it settles into flowering. Once established in a cool, sheltered bed it is long-lived and needs little routine care beyond protecting it from summer drought and winter wet.
